1. Background
This circular reiterates mandatory exposure control measures for personnel working in or near the Benzene storage and loading area (TK-701 to TK-704) within the Aromatic Complex. Benzene is classified as a Category 1 carcinogen. All requirements below are mandatory and supersede general area PPE guidance for this specific zone.

Exposure Metric	Limit	Action if Exceeded
8-hour TWA (Time Weighted Average)	1 ppm	Immediate area evacuation, HSE incident report within 4 hours
Short-Term Exposure Limit (STEL, 15 min)	5 ppm	Area evacuation, personal monitor review
Fixed gas detector alarm threshold	0.5 ppm	Automatic area alarm + PA announcement
3. Mandatory Controls
Personal benzene dosimeter badges worn at all times within the tank farm boundary, logged out/in at the HSE gate register.
Supplied-air respiratory protection required for any tank-top gauging, sampling, or connection/disconnection of loading arms.
No hot work within 30 metres of TK-701 to TK-704 without an active Hot Work Permit co-signed by the Aromatic Complex Shift Supervisor and HSE.
Continuous fixed benzene detection required to be in-service before any loading operation commences; loading is prohibited if any detector in the zone is under maintenance without an approved compensatory monitoring plan.

Chapter No: 1
Introduction
1.1 Overview of the Policy
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 15 August, 2014 announced "Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana
(PMJDY)" which is a National Mission for Financial Inclusion.The task is gigantic and is a National
Priority. This National Mission on Financial Inclusion has an ambitious objective of covering all
households in the country with banking facilities and having a bank account for each household. It has
been emphasised by the Hon'ble PM that this is important for including people left-out into the
mainstream of the financial system. The Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana will be launched on 28
August, 2014, across the nation simultaneously. It will be launched formally in Delhi with parallel
functions at the state level and also at district and sub-district levels. Camps are also to be organized at
the branch level. The Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana lies at the core of the development philosophy
of "Sab Ka Sath Sab Ka Vikas". With a bank account, every household would gain access to banking
and credit facilities. This will enable them to come out of the grip of moneylenders, manage to keep
away from financial crises caused by emergent needs, and most importantly, benefit from a range of
financial products. As a first step, every account holder gets a RuPay debit card with a 1,00,000/-
accident cover. Further, they will be covered by insurance and pension products. There is a need to
enroll over 7.5 crore households and open their accounts.
Earlier efforts by the Government of India included setting up a committee on financial inclusion
under the chairmanship of Dr. C. Rangarajan. The committee finalized its report in early 2008. As is
evident from the preamble of the report, the committee interpreted financial inclusion as an
instrumentality for social transformation. "Access to finance by the poor and vulnerable groups is a
prerequisite for inclusive growth. In fact, providing access to finance is a form of empowerment of the
vulnerable groups. Financial Inclusion denotes delivery of financial services at an affordable cost to

Even after decades of bank nationalization, whose rationale was to shift the focus from class banking
to mass banking, we still find usurious money lenders in rural areas and urban slums continuing to
exploit the poor. After economic reforms of 1991, the country can ill-afford not to include the poor in
the growth paradigm. Financial Inclusion of the poor will help in bringing them to the mainstream of
growth and would also provide the Financial Institutions an opportunity to be partners in inclusive
growth.
Experiences in India and abroad have shown that traditional Banks have struggled to reach the poor
with financial services. Recognizing this fact, many countries such as Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia,
Mexico etc. have allowed non-banks to offer payments, deposits and cash-in/cash-out services.
Similarly, in India, enabling an inclusive competitive landscape should be a top priority.
India has several strategic assets providing favourable initial conditions for transformational change
towards digital financial inclusion:
● A strong banking network (1,15,000 branches) linked to eKuber (RBI's Core Banking
Solution), now spreading into unbanked rural areas.
● A significant outreach of India Post (1,55,000 outlets), PoS and ATM terminals which can
facilitate a vibrant cash-in/cash-out network across the country.
● A nation-wide telecom network with 886 million mobile connections and 72% mobile
penetration.
● Strong Network of computer based service providers in the form of Common Service Centres
(CSC) promoted by Deptt of IT.
● A strong national payments infrastructure that includes an Inter-Mobile Payments Service /
Immediate Payment System (IMPS) to transfer funds over mobile phones.
● A world class national ID system covering the largest (650M) headcount and expanding by
30M citizens per month.
Objective of "Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)" is ensuring access to various
financial services like availability of basic savings bank account, access to need based credit,
remittances facility, insurance and pension to the excluded sections i.e. weaker sections &
low income groups. This deep penetration at affordable cost is possible only with effective
use of technology.

The objective of this case study is to conduct a comprehensive overview of the Pradhan Mantri Jan
Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) as an initiative for advancing national financial inclusion in India. Launched
to bridge the divide between the formal backing system and the unbanked population, the scheme
aims to ensure universal access to financial services including basic savings accounts, remittable
credit, insurance and pension facilities at an affordable cost.
This study examines the operational efficiency, reach and overall socioeconomic impact of PMJDY
since its starting. It evaluates how successfully the initiative has shifted the banking paradigm from
high cost , urban centric “class banking” to scalable, accessible “mass banking.” . The study explores
the role of digital infrastructure, such as the Jan Dhan Aadhaar Mobile (JAM) trinity and the business
correspondent (Bank Mitra) network, in driving account usage, enabling Direct Benefit transfers
(DBT) and reducing dependency on informal, predatory money lenders. Ultimately, this research aims
to identify key operational challenges, evaluate the sustainability of zero balance accounts, and
provide recommendations to strengthen rural financial ecosystems, enhance digital literacy, and foster
long term economic empowerment for low income households across the country.

PMJDY to be executed in the Mission Mode, envisages provision of affordable financial services to
all citizens within a reasonable distance. It comprises of the following six pillars:-
a. Universal access to banking facilities: Mapping of each district into Sub Service Area (SSA)
catering to 1000-1500 households in a manner that every habitation has access to banking services
within a reasonable distance say 5 km by 14th August, 2015. Coverage of parts of J&K, Himachal
Pradesh, Uttarakhand, North East and the Left Wing Extremism affected districts which have telecom
connectivity and infrastructure constraints would spill over to the Phase II of the program (15th
August, 2015 to 15th August, 2018)
b. Providing Basic Banking Accounts with overdraft facility and RuPay Debit card to all households:
The effort would be to first cover all uncovered households with banking facilities by August, 2015,
by opening basic bank accounts. Account holders would be provided a RuPay Debit Card. Facility of
an overdraft to every basic banking account holder would be considered after satisfactory operation /
credit history of six months.
c. Financial Literacy Programme: Financial literacy would be an integral part of the Mission in order
to let the beneficiaries make best use of the financial services being made available to them.
d. Creation of Credit Guarantee Fund: Creation of a Credit Guarantee Fund would be to cover the
defaults in overdraft accounts.
e. Micro-Insurance: To provide micro-insurance to all willing and eligible persons by 14th August,
2018, and then on an ongoing basis.

The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana relies on a multi stakeholder framework that includes
government entities, financial institutions and grassroots networks.
At the top level, the Ministry of Finance(Government of India) and the Reserve Bank of India(RBI)
act as primary architects, establishing policy directives, regulatory guidelines and oversight
mechanisms. Implementation is done by Public Sector Banks, Regional Rural Banks and Private
Sector Banks which bear the operational responsibility of opening basic savings accounts, issuing
RuPay debit cards and providing credit facilities like overdrafts.
An important operational layer is the Business Correspondent(BC) network, of Bank Mitras, Acting
as last mile infrastructure these local agents including kirana store owners, telecom outlets and self
help group members bring branchless banking directly to remote unbanked habitations.
Technological and Identity Infrastructure partners are also vital. The Unique Identification Authority
of India (UIDAI) enables biometric authentication via Aadhaar for seamless e-KYC account creation,
while the National Payments corporation of India powers the digital payment backbone through the
Aadhaar payment bridge system and immediate payment service(IMPS). Additionally, India Post
expands physical reach through its extensive nationwide network.

The launch of the Prandhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) in 2014 was driven by the structural

remained entirely detached from the formal banking sector.
A primary cause was the failure of earlier initiatives to achieve last mile financial penetration. As of

centers due to high operational costs, making rural outreach economically unviable. Millions of poor
households in rural areas and urban slums relied on local, informal money lenders who exploited them
with high interest rates, trapping generations in debt cycles.

4.3 Role of Technology
Technology and financial inclusion are the popular coinage in banking parlance in the country. Main
hurdle in financial inclusion so far has been large numbers and low volumes, translating into
unaffordable costs. The only way to bring down the cost to an affordable level and to improve the
reach to the farthest / remotest corner of the country is by effectively leveraging the Technology. In
order to make available the banking facilities across the length and breadth of the country, latest
technological products like e-KYC, IMPS, AEPS, mobile banking etc. have the potential to emerge as
a game changer in terms of costs, convenience, and speed of reach. Business models of banks,
telecom operators and other stakeholders need to converge. Under the guidance of RBI various
organisations like National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), Institute for Development &
Research in Banking Technology (IDRBT) etc. are contributing significantly in bringing new
technology based products. Reserve Bank has, thus, been actively involved in harnessing technology
for the development of the Indian banking sector over the years.
(i) Electronically Know Your Customer (e-KYC).
In the year 2013, RBI permitted e-KYC as a valid process for KYC verification under Prevention of
Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005. In order to reduce the risk of identity
fraud, documentary forgery and have paperless KYC verification, UIDAI has launched its e-KYC
services. Under the e-KYC process under the explicit consent of the customer and after his or her
biometric authentication from UIDAI database individual basic data comprising name, age, gender
and photograph can be shared electronically with Authorised Users like Banks, which is a valid
process for KYC.
(ii) Transaction through Mobile Banking:
The mobile-phone revolution that is transforming the country could also turn into a banking
revolution in terms of reach and transaction. Today, the number of mobiles in India is 886 million.

coverage of mobile phones and the use of such instruments by all section of the population can be

(iii) Immediate Payment System (IMPS): Immediate Payment Service (IMPS) was launched by NPCI

(iv) Micro-ATMs: Micro-ATMs are biometric authentication enabled hand-held device. In order to

SOP-114: Hydrocracker Catalyst Changeout Procedure
Document No: SOP-114-Rev3   |   Unit: Hydrocracker-2 (HCU-2)   |   Effective Date: 2026-03-14   |   Review Cycle: 24 months
1. Purpose
This procedure defines the safe sequence of operations for changing out spent hydrocracking catalyst in HCU-2 Reactor R-201, including bed unloading, sulfiding of fresh catalyst, and return-to-service checks. This SOP applies specifically to the NiMo-alumina extrudate catalyst system currently qualified for HCU-2 service.
2. Scope and Applicability
Applies to: HCU-2 Reactor R-201 (Beds 1-3), associated recycle gas compressor K-201, and feed/effluent heat exchanger train E-201A/B. Does not apply to HCU-1 (R-101), which uses a different catalyst loading pattern under SOP-098.
3. Key Process Parameters (Reference Values)
The table below lists the normal operating envelope used to judge catalyst end-of-run:
Parameter	Normal Range	End-of-Run Trigger	Unit
Weighted Average Bed Temperature (WABT)	365 - 385	> 410	°C
LHSV (Liquid Hourly Space Velocity)	1.1 - 1.4	N/A (design basis)	hr⁻¹
Reactor Delta-P (Bed 2)	0.8 - 1.5	> 3.5	kg/cm²
Conversion (360°C+ fraction)	68 - 72	< 60	%
Recycle Gas H2 Purity	92 - 95	< 88	%
Catalyst Cycle Length (design)	22 - 26	N/A	months
4. Changeout Sequence
4.1 Unit shutdown and depressurization of R-201 per SOP-050 (Reactor Depressurization).
4.2 Nitrogen purge to < 0.5% hydrocarbon (LEL meter confirmation) before vessel entry permit is issued.
4.3 Spent catalyst unloading via vacuum system, Beds 1-3 in sequence, with continuous H2S monitoring in the confined space.
4.4 Internals inspection: distributor trays, quench zones, thermocouple wells - findings logged on Form F-114-A.

4.3 Spent catalyst unloading via vacuum system, Beds 1-3 in sequence, with continuous H2S monitoring in the confined space.
4.4 Internals inspection: distributor trays, quench zones, thermocouple wells - findings logged on Form F-114-A.
4.5 Fresh catalyst loading (dense loading method) to the bed density specified in the catalyst vendor's Technical Data Sheet, batch-verified against the Certificate of Analysis.
4.6 Catalyst sulfiding (activation) per the sulfiding curve in Appendix A - typical duration 36-48 hours.
4.7 Gradual introduction of feed, WABT ramp not exceeding 15°C/hour until target conversion is reached.
4.8 Post-changeout performance verification against Section 3 parameters for 72 continuous hours before the unit is declared in normal service.
5. Safety Precautions
Pyrophoric catalyst hazard: spent NiMo catalyst can self-heat on air exposure. Unloading must proceed under continuous nitrogen blanket or water-wetting per vendor guidance. Full-face supplied-air respirators are mandatory for all vessel-entry personnel. H2S monitoring is continuous throughout Sections 4.3-4.4.

## Agentic tool calling — NEW, and the current quality gap is mine

**Built:** `backend/orchestrator/agent_loop.py` + `POST /api/chat/stream`.
A real tool-calling loop using Ollama's native function calling
(verified with qwen2.5:7b): the model sees the registry, chooses a tool,
gets the result back in the conversation, and continues — narrating
throughout. Every step is an event; the protocol is
`docs/Technical_Specs/AGENT_STREAM_PROTOCOL.md`.

This closed a real hole. `dispatch_node` chose tools with a hardcoded
if/elif on agent type, so 17 registered tools with derived schemas were
unreachable — the model never CHOSE anything. Hard constraint #3 ("no
math without a tool call") held only for the one arithmetic path wired
by hand.

**And it exposed a bigger one:** there was no search tool. The registry's
"retrieval" category held `find_contradictions` and
`select_images_for_request`, so it looked populated, while hybrid search
— the thing the whole product rests on — was reachable only from inside
`dispatch_node`. Given the full registry and asked for a value printed
in the corpus, the model called `find_contradictions`, got `[]`, and
reported that no document contained it. Fixed:
`backend/tools/retrieval_tools.py` registers `search_documents` and
`list_documents`.

**MY OPEN ITEM, stated plainly:** answer quality on the streaming path
is currently WORSE than `/api/chat`. The loop retrieves correctly and
then under-extracts — the direct path answers "3.4 g/10min [1]"
consistently where the loop retrieved the right documents and said it
could not find the value. The difference is scaffolding, not mechanism:
`/api/chat` applies a grounding prompt tuned against measured failures
(citation form, answer depth, refusal wording) and the loop hands raw
passages to a 7B with a general system prompt.

Until that closes: `/api/chat` is the default answering path,
`/api/chat/stream` is the agentic one, and Netal builds the thinking UI
against the stream knowing this.

Also mine: tool-selection reliability. Offering all 19 tools to a 7B
produced `lookup_thermophysical_property` called five times drifting
into the density of methane. Curating `CHAT_TOOLS` fixed it; that
curation is a workaround for a model-size limit and should be revisited
on venue hardware.

### 4b. Multi-hop graph traversal visualisation — **NEW, and the demo moment**

The interesting GraphRAG questions are not "show me this node", they are
multi-hop: *"what incidents touch the segment this SOP governs?"* is
Document -> PipelineSegment -> Incident. **The answer is the path, not
the endpoints**, and a path is something you can only really show by
animating it.

Backend ready (built for you): `GET /api/graph/neighbourhood?node=X&hops=N`
returns the subgraph within N hops, and **every node carries its
`distance`** plus a `by_distance` histogram. Verified live:

```
'Mangalore-Hassan' hops=1: 3 nodes,  4 edges, by_distance={'0':1, '1':2}
'Mangalore-Hassan' hops=2: 8 nodes, 18 edges, by_distance={'0':1, '1':2, '2':5}
'P-HS-02'          hops=2: 5 nodes, 10 edges, by_distance={'0':1, '1':1, '2':3}
```

`distance` exists specifically so you can stage the reveal: hop 0, then
hop 1, then hop 2. A traversal that appears all at once is a hairball; a
traversal that unfolds is an explanation, and it is the clearest
possible demonstration that this system reasons over connections rather
than just matching text.

What to build:
- **Hop-by-hop reveal** on query. Ring 0 is the anchor, then each hop
  fades in with its edges. Let the user step forward and back.
- **Path highlight** between two selected nodes — trace the actual
  route, dim everything else.
- **Hop depth control** (1-4, the API caps it) so the user can widen or
  narrow the neighbourhood live.
- **Edge types on the path**, always visible. `REFERENCES` vs
  `REPORTS_INCIDENT_AT` is the difference between "this document
  mentions the segment" and "an incident happened there", and hiding the
  distinction makes the graph decorative.
- **Wire it to the chat**: when an answer cites documents, offer "show
  how these connect" and traverse from them.

- The graph has been **lost three times** to a container without a named

### 4c. Granular agent thinking UI — **NEW, isolated partition, highest ceiling**

The app answers after 17-25 seconds of silence. What it should do is
what a good agent does: say what it is about to do, do it, say what it
got, move on. Text, work, text, work.

**The backend for this is built and streaming today.** `POST /api/chat/stream`
emits Server-Sent Events as the agent works — narration token by token,
each tool call *before* it runs with its arguments, each result with its
real return value and duration. Full contract:
`docs/Technical_Specs/AGENT_STREAM_PROTOCOL.md`.

A measured turn produced **173 events**. This is yours to render.

What to build:
- **Interleaved transcript** in arrival order. Narration, then the call,
  then the result, then more narration. Do not batch the tool calls to
  the end — the order *is* the explanation.
- **In-flight tool state.** Show the call the moment it is emitted, with
  a spinner, then fill in the result. The gap between them is where the
  work happens and it is often seconds.
- **Arguments always visible, output collapsed by default.**
- **Failed-call recovery rendering.** A tool that fails gets fed back to
  the model, which usually retries. Render repeated calls as a sequence,
  not by replacing the previous one. A failed tool is not a failed turn.
- **Approval interception.** `approval_required` means the loop stopped
  and the tool did NOT run. Show the modal; do not render the turn as
  finished.

**Why showing arguments is a safety feature, not a debug nicety.**
Measured: asked for "381.95 minus 400", the model called
`evaluate_expression("-381.95 - 400")` — a spurious leading minus — and
the tool correctly computed -781.95 for the expression it was given. The
answer arrives with a genuine tool-call receipt attached. Nothing
downstream can tell it is wrong. **A human seeing the arguments is the
only thing that catches it.** That makes your UI a correctness control,
not decoration.

**Read the "Known limitation" section of the protocol before you start.**
Answer quality on this endpoint is currently worse than `/api/chat` —
the loop retrieves correctly and then under-extracts. That is Aryan's to
close. You are building the surface; don't be surprised by the answers.

Buffer the `text_delta` events before rendering — token-level fragments
at 173 events per turn will thrash React otherwise.

## 2b. Fetch the local models — DO THIS FIRST ON A NEW MACHINE

```bash
py -3 -m backend.ingestion.fetch_models
```

Needs internet **once**. After that the system is fully offline — every
model-backed tool loads only from `models/<category>/` and never checks
a hub.

**Why this is not optional, and why forgetting it is dangerous.**
`models/embeddings/` is **gitignored** (1.3 GB), so it does NOT arrive
with a `git pull`. Without it, embeddings fall back to hash vectors,
which carry no semantic meaning — and nothing appears broken. Searches
return results. Answers carry citations. The content is simply wrong.

This happened on a teammate's machine. Asked for one person's
assignments, retrieval returned two other people's files and the answer
described a third person entirely. Adding a single backslash to the
query changed the whole result set, because hash vectors have no notion
of meaning for a typo to survive.

**How to tell:**
```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/api/health
```
`embedding_backend` must read `bge-large-en-v1.5`. If it says
`deterministic-hash`, retrieval is meaningless — the backend also logs a
large warning at startup and on every affected turn.

# AGENT_STREAM_PROTOCOL.md — the contract between the agent loop and the UI

**Owners:** Aryan (backend, `backend/orchestrator/agent_loop.py`) ·
Netal (frontend rendering)

This is the wire format for the interleaved "text, work, text, work"
experience — the agent saying what it is about to do, doing it, saying
what it got, and continuing. It is a contract: neither side changes an
event shape without changing this file.

---

## Endpoint

```
POST /api/chat/stream
Content-Type: application/json
{ "message": "...", "session_id": "..." }

-> text/event-stream
   data: {"type": "...", ...}\n\n
```

Standard SSE. Each `data:` line is one complete JSON event. The stream
ends after a `done` or `error` event.

---

## Events

### `start`
```json
{"type": "start", "request": "What is the SOP for catalyst changeout?"}
```
First event, always. Use it to clear any previous state.

### `text_delta`
```json
{"type": "text_delta", "text": " the SOP for"}
```
A fragment of the agent's narration, as the model produces it. Append
in order. These arrive **between** tool calls as well as at the end —
that interleaving is the whole point of this endpoint.

Fragments are token-level, so expect many (a measured turn produced 173
events). Buffer before rendering if that is too many React updates.

### `tool_call`
```json
{"type": "tool_call", "id": "call_287cqkr5",
 "name": "search_documents",
 "arguments": {"query": "SOP hydrocracker catalyst changeout", "top_k": 5}}
```
Emitted **before** the tool runs, so the UI can show it as in-flight.

**Render the arguments. This is a safety feature, not a debug detail.**
Measured: asked for "381.95 minus 400", the model called
`evaluate_expression` with `"-381.95 - 400"` — a spurious leading minus
— and the tool correctly returned `-781.95` for the expression it was
given. Hard constraint #3 guarantees the number came from an executed
tool. It does **not** guarantee the model asked the right question, and
nothing downstream can tell the difference: the wrong answer arrives
with a genuine tool-call receipt attached.

The only thing that catches this is a human seeing `-381.95 - 400` on
screen. Show the arguments.

### `tool_result`
```json
{"type": "tool_result", "id": "call_287cqkr5", "name": "search_documents",
 "output": {"found": true, "passages": [...]},
 "status": "done", "seconds": 0.14}
```
`status` is `done` or `failed`. A `failed` result carries
`output.error` and is fed back to the model, which may retry — so
expect repeated calls to the same tool, and render them as a sequence
rather than replacing the previous one.

`output` is the tool's real return value, converted to JSON without
flattening structure. Collapse it by default; an engineer wants it on
demand, not in their face.

### `approval_required`
```json
{"type": "approval_required", "id": "call_x", "name": "draft_docx",
 "arguments": {...}, "effect": "Draft a DOCX report..."}
```
The loop **stops here**. The tool has not run. Hard constraint #4: no
file write, send, or SAP write without a human gate.

A `done` event with `"awaiting_approval": true` follows immediately.
Show the approval modal; do not render the turn as finished.

### `done`
```json
{"type": "done", "reply": "full narration text", "tool_calls": 3,
 "iterations": 2, "seconds": 48.17, "awaiting_approval": false}
```
`reply` is the concatenation of every `text_delta`. Use it to replace
your accumulated buffer once, rather than trusting your own
concatenation.

### `error`
```json
{"type": "error", "message": "The model call failed: ..."}
```
Render it. A stream that stops without an event is indistinguishable
from a slow one, so a silent truncation leaves the UI spinning forever
— which is why a crash mid-stream is converted into this event.

---

## Rendering guidance

1. **Interleave in arrival order.** Narration, then the call, then the
   result, then more narration. Do not group all tool calls together at
   the end; the order is the explanation.
2. **Show the tool call before the result**, in a pending state. The
   gap between them is where the work happens and is often seconds.
3. **Show arguments always, output on demand.** See `tool_call` above.
4. **A failed tool is not a failed turn.** The agent frequently
   recovers. Style it as an event, not an error state.
5. **Do not invent progress.** No fake percentage, no synthetic steps.
   This codebase shipped a "Retrieving sources · 21s" indicator that
   counted forever with no request behind it; that is the failure mode
   to avoid.

---

## Routing — the backend chooses the path, not the UI

**`POST /api/chat/stream` is the only endpoint the UI needs.** It routes
the request and emits the same event protocol whichever path answers, so
the frontend renders one shape and never decides anything.

The `route` event, second in every stream, says which path ran and why:

```json
{"type": "route", "path": "direct",
 "reason": "Single-intent lookup — one retrieval and a grounded answer...",
 "tools_expected": false}
```

The `route` event, second in every stream, says which path ran and why:

```json
{"type": "route", "path": "direct",
 "reason": "Single-intent lookup — one retrieval and a grounded answer...",
 "tools_expected": false}
```

| `path` | When | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `corpus` | "what documents do you have", "summarise your data" | Answered from the source index. No model, no retrieval, nothing that can be fabricated |
| `direct` | Single-intent lookup — "what is the MFI for H030SG?", "what is the SOP for catalyst changeout?" | One retrieval, one grounded answer with the tuned citation/refusal scaffolding. Emits a `search_documents` tool call so the UI shows the same detail as the agentic path |
| `agentic` | Multi-step, comparison, computation, actions — "project when delta-P crosses the trigger", "compare these and draft a report" | The loop: model chooses tools, runs them, reads results, continues |

Routing is structural (`backend/orchestrator/path_router.py`) — it reuses
`is_simple_lookup`, the same classifier that decides whether to skip the
planner, so the two cannot disagree about the same property. It is not a
model call: that would cost as much as a short answer and add a failure
mode where the router itself is unreachable. **It fails towards
`direct`**, the path with better answer quality and full grounding
scaffolding.

Measured 10/10 on the routing cases.

**Why this matters for your UI:** `direct` and `corpus` answers arrive as
one `text_delta`, not token by token, because those paths are not
streamed. That is deliberate — faking a typewriter over an answer that
already exists is inventing progress, which is the failure mode the
deleted "Retrieving sources · 21s" indicator embodied. Render a single
delta as a complete message; do not wait for more.

### Consider showing the route

The `reason` is written to be shown. A user who sees *"multi-step or
needs computation — the agent will choose tools"* understands why this
answer is taking 40 seconds when the last one took 8. A routing decision
nobody can see is one nobody can question.

### Answer quality, honestly

The agentic loop under-extracts on plain lookups — it retrieves the
right documents and then fails to pull the value out. **Routing largely
removes this in practice**, because lookups now go to `direct`, which is
where the grounding scaffolding lives.

It still applies to genuinely multi-step requests, which have no
alternative path. Closing that gap is Aryan's, tracked in
`docs/STATUS.md`.

## Tool set offered in chat

Curated, not the whole registry — `CHAT_TOOLS` in `agent_loop.py`:

```
search_documents  list_documents  evaluate_expression
evaluate_unit_expression  analyse_trend  project_to_threshold
describe_series  select_images_for_request  extract_printed_text
```

Offering all 19 registered tools to a 7B model was measured producing:
`find_contradictions` called with empty arguments (it returns `[]`,
which reads as "nothing found"); `lookup_thermophysical_property`
called five times with wrong arguments, drifting into the density of
methane; and `search_documents` emitted as literal text instead of as a
call. Selection accuracy falls off with option count, and a loop
compounds it — a wrong first choice becomes the context for every
choice after it.

Excluded tools are **not disabled**. They remain registered, tested,
and callable through `POST /api/tools/call`. They are simply not
offered as a free choice mid-conversation.

# AGENTS_SPEC.md — Complete Multi-Agent Orchestration Specification

## 1. Framework
LangGraph (Python). The orchestrator is an explicit state graph, not a single long prompt loop — this is what makes the plan visible and inspectable in the frontend (FRONTEND.md §3.4), and what makes FR-5 demoable rather than just claimed.

## 2. State Object (exact shape, shared across all nodes)

```python
class AgentState(BaseModel):
    session_id: str
    original_request: str
    plan: list[PlanStep]
    current_step_index: int
    tool_call_log: list[ToolCallEvent]
    retrieved_context: list[RetrievedChunk]   # from RAG_SPEC.md
    draft_output: str | None
    verification_result: VerificationResult | None
    awaiting_human_approval: bool
    final_output_path: str | None

class PlanStep(BaseModel):
    step_id: str
    description: str
    assigned_agent: Literal["vision", "code", "reasoning", "math", "retrieval"]
    status: Literal["pending", "running", "done", "failed"]
    depends_on: list[str]   # step_ids that must complete first

class ToolCallEvent(BaseModel):
    tool_name: str
    input_params: dict
    output: dict | None
    status: Literal["pending", "running", "done", "failed"]
    timestamp: str
```

## 3. Graph Nodes (exact node names — the frontend's plan graph reads these directly, keep them stable)

```
[router] → [planner] → [dispatch] → {vision_agent | code_agent | reasoning_agent | math_tool | retrieval_agent}
                                              │
                                              ▼
                                    [verify] → [approval_gate] → [output_writer] → [END]
                                              │
                                    (if verification fails)
                                              ▼
                                         [planner] (re-plan, max 2 retries)
```

- **`router`**: calls CARD 03's `classify_task`, populates `AgentState.original_request`'s task tags
- **`planner`**: given task tags + `original_request`, calls the reasoning sub-agent with a plan-decomposition prompt (exact template below), populates `AgentState.plan` as a `PlanStep` list
- **`dispatch`**: reads `AgentState.plan`, for each step whose `depends_on` are all `done`, routes to the matching sub-agent node — this enables parallel execution of independent steps, not strictly sequential
- **`verify`**: calls the self-verification agent (phi-3.5-mini) with the exact prompt below
- **`approval_gate`**: sets `awaiting_human_approval = True`, halts graph execution (LangGraph's interrupt mechanism) until the frontend posts a confirm/cancel back to the backend
- **`output_writer`**: calls the relevant output-generation tool (CARD 06 etc.), sets `final_output_path`

## 4. Exact Planner Prompt

```
You are a task planner for an industrial AI assistant. Given the request below, produce a JSON list of steps. Each step must have: "step_id" (short unique string), "description" (one sentence), "assigned_agent" (one of "vision", "code", "reasoning", "math", "retrieval"), "depends_on" (list of step_ids that must complete first, empty list if none).

Only include steps that are actually necessary. Do not add speculative steps beyond what the request requires.

REQUEST:
{original_request}
```

## 5. Exact Verification Prompt

```
You are checking whether an AI assistant's output actually satisfies the original request. Answer with a JSON object: {"satisfied": true/false, "reason": "one sentence explanation", "missing": ["list of anything missing, empty if satisfied is true"]}.

ORIGINAL REQUEST:
{original_request}

PRODUCED OUTPUT:
{draft_output}
```

If `satisfied: false`, route back to `planner` with the `missing` list appended to context, up to a **maximum of 2 re-plan cycles** — after 2 failed verifications, halt and surface the issue to the human via the approval gate UI with an explicit "verification could not confirm this output is complete" flag, rather than looping indefinitely or silently shipping an unverified result.

## 6. Sub-Agent Contracts (what each node is allowed and forbidden to do)

| Sub-agent | Allowed | Forbidden |
|---|---|---|
| `vision_agent` | Call OCR/VLM/ASR tools (CARD 05, CARD 12, etc.), return extracted text/structure. Scope deliberately broadened beyond pure vision to cover audio transcription (CARD 12, a team addition — see REQUIREMENTS.md §6) rather than introduce a new sub-agent/enum value for one tool; "vision_agent" here means "extraction from a non-text-native input modality," not literally "only images." | Cannot call code execution or write files directly |
| `code_agent` | Call CARD 04 sandbox execution, iterate on failure up to 3 attempts | Cannot execute outside the sandbox under any circumstance |
| `reasoning_agent` | Draft text, call retrieval for grounding | Cannot state a fact without a citation if retrieval was available for that domain (enforced per RAG_SPEC.md §4) |
| `math_tool` | Call SymPy/NumPy/etc. directly (not an LLM call at all — a direct function call node) | N/A — this node never invokes an LLM, by design, per NFR-5 |
| `retrieval_agent` | Call hybrid_search (CARD 09) | Cannot fabricate a chunk if retrieval returns nothing — must return the explicit "not found" signal per RAG_SPEC.md §3 |

## 7. Human Approval Gate — Exact Trigger Conditions

The `approval_gate` node is mandatory (cannot be bypassed by any config flag) before:
1. Any `output_writer` call that writes a file to a persistent location
2. Any action that would constitute a "send" (email, external system call) — though no such action is in scope for the 10-day build per REQUIREMENTS.md §4, the gate exists in the architecture so this is a config addition later, not a redesign
3. Any SAP write action (out of scope for this build, but the gate is architecturally where it would attach)

## 8. Checkpointing (🟡 tier)
LangGraph's built-in checkpointer (SQLite backend) persists `AgentState` after every node transition, so a long-running task can be resumed after a pause without replaying completed steps. Implement this once the core graph (§3) is stable — do not let checkpointing complexity block the core loop's Day 1-2 delivery.

## 9. Testing Requirements
- A test that runs a full graph execution for a mocked multi-step request and asserts: plan has ≥2 steps, dispatch correctly parallelizes independent steps, verify triggers a re-plan when the mocked output is deliberately incomplete, approval_gate correctly halts execution until an external confirm signal is sent
- A test asserting the `math_tool` node never constructs an LLM API call — grep/mock-assert this directly, since it's a hard architectural guarantee (NFR-5), not just an expected behavior

## 1. Design Philosophy

Three reference products, three things borrowed from each, deliberately:

| From | What we borrow | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude (chatbot)** | Calm, uncluttered chat surface. Generous whitespace. Warm neutral palette, not corporate-cold blue-and-white. Messages feel like they're being *composed*, not printed. | This is the primary interaction surface — it needs to feel trustworthy and unhurried, appropriate for drafting an approval note, not like a stock trading terminal |
| **Claude Code** | Visible, inspectable agent reasoning. A plan/task list the user can watch execute step by step. Tool calls shown as discrete, collapsible events, not buried in a wall of text. | This is what proves "agentic," not just "chatbot" — judges need to *see* the plan-execute-verify loop happening |
| **NotebookLM** | A visible "sources" panel — always present, always showing exactly what's grounding the current session. Citations that expand inline to show the exact source passage. A sense of "this notebook only knows what you gave it." | This is the trust mechanism — critical for an approval-note tool in a safety-critical industry |

**Visual tone:** warm off-white/cream background (not stark white), deep charcoal text (not pure black), one confident accent color used sparingly (a muted terracotta/rust or deep amber works well against the industrial/refinery subject matter without being literal "hazard orange"), generous rounded corners (12-16px), soft shadows, no gradients as decoration (gradients only where they communicate something, e.g. a live/active state pulse). Typography: a humanist sans (Inter or similar) for UI chrome, a serif or slab for document previews (DOCX/PPTX previews should look like documents, not like app screens).

**Motion principle:** every state change animates, nothing snaps. Plan graph nodes animate from "pending" → "in progress" (pulsing) → "done" (settle + checkmark). Citations expand with a smooth height transition. The network monitor's live connection count should tick, not jump. This is what makes the demo feel "otherworldly" rather than "functional" — motion communicates that the system is alive and working, not static.

# GRAPH_SPEC.md — Complete Knowledge Graph Specification

## 1. Purpose
Plain vector retrieval cannot answer "show every SOP referencing this valve" or "what maintenance records and incident reports touch the Hassan pumping station segment" — these are graph-shaped questions. This document specifies the exact schema so the graph is buildable without guesswork.

## 2. Storage Choice
**Locked: Neo4j Community Edition.** Cypher query language, mature visualization tooling, and this is now the only graph backend implemented — no NetworkX fallback path to build or maintain. Every Cypher example in this document is the actual implementation target, not a placeholder.

**Hard constraint, verified by actually running the default Docker image:** Neo4j's default config sends anonymous usage telemetry on every startup — its own log prints "Anonymous Usage Data is being sent to Neo4j" unless disabled. This is exactly the kind of default phone-home behavior CLAUDE.md's hard constraint #1 requires auditing every dependency for. It is NOT disabled by default — whoever builds the real `docker-compose.yml` (SYSTEM.md §5 / DEPENDENCIES.md §10) MUST set `NEO4J_dbms_usage__report_enabled=false` as an environment variable on the Neo4j container. Confirmed fixed: the exact same container with this flag set produces a clean startup log with no telemetry line at all.

**Second hard constraint, paid for directly during development, not theoretical:** a Neo4j container started with `docker run` and no volume mount keeps its data ONLY in that container's own writable layer. When the dev environment this was built in got recycled, the container came back with zero nodes — roughly 40 minutes of real LLM-driven entity extraction (GRAPH_SPEC.md §5) was gone, with no way to recover it short of re-running every extraction call. Every Neo4j container this project ever starts — dev, portable-drive demo, real MRPL deployment — MUST mount a named volume for `/data`:
```
docker run -d --name <container> \
  -v <volume-name>:/data \
  -e NEO4J_AUTH=neo4j/<password> \
  -e NEO4J_dbms_usage__report_enabled=false \
  neo4j:5-community
```
This is necessary but not sufficient on its own — see `backend/evaluation/extract_corpus.py`'s module docstring for the other half of the actual fix: the expensive part of graph construction (LLM extraction) is now checkpointed to a durable JSON Lines file on disk BEFORE anything touches Neo4j at all, so even total loss of the graph database costs a few seconds to recover from (reload the checkpoint), never another 40 minutes of re-extraction.

## 3. Node Types (exact labels, do not invent variants)

| Label | Properties | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Document` | `id`, `filename`, `document_type`, `ingestion_date` | SOP-114-Rev3.pdf |
| `Equipment` | `id`, `tag`, `unit` (e.g. "Hydrocracker-2", "CCR-1"), `equipment_type` (valve, pump, vessel, etc.) | Valve V-204 |
| `PipelineSegment` | `id`, `segment_name`, `start_point`, `end_point` | "Mangalore-Hassan" |
| `Person` | `id`, `name`, `role` (extracted from correspondence/sign-off blocks only — never inferred) | — |
| `Incident` | `id`, `date`, `severity`, `summary` | — |
| `MaintenanceRecord` | `id`, `date`, `equipment_ref`, `action_taken` | from SAP Maintenance module data via the SAP connector |

## 4. Relationship Types (exact labels)

| Relationship | From → To | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `REFERENCES` | `Document` → `Equipment` / `PipelineSegment` | The document mentions this entity |
| `SUPERSEDES` | `Document` → `Document` | Revision N supersedes revision N-1 |
| `APPLIES_TO` | `Document` → `Equipment` / `PipelineSegment` | The SOP's scope explicitly covers this entity (stronger than REFERENCES — extracted from explicit "applicability" sections, not just mentions) |
| `LOCATED_ON` | `Equipment` → `PipelineSegment` | Physical association |
| `AUTHORED_BY` | `Document` → `Person` | Sign-off/authorship |
| `REPORTS_INCIDENT_AT` | `Incident` → `Equipment` / `PipelineSegment` | — |
| `MAINTENANCE_PERFORMED_ON` | `MaintenanceRecord` → `Equipment` | From SAP-sourced data |

## 4.1 Extraction-to-Schema Property Bridge (gap found while implementing, not in the original spec)

§5's extraction prompt asks the LLM for a generic `{"type": ..., "name": string, "attributes": object}` shape for every entity type — but §3's node schema uses a DIFFERENT key property name per type (`tag` for Equipment, `segment_name` for PipelineSegment, `name` for Person, and Incident has no name-like field at all — just `date`/`severity`/`summary`). Nothing in the original spec bridged these, which only became visible when actually wiring extraction output into `MERGE` statements. The bridge, fixed here so it's a documented decision instead of a silent code-only choice:

| Extracted `type` | §3 key property to `MERGE` on | Extraction's `name` value goes into |
|---|---|---|
| `Equipment` | `tag` | the `tag` property |
| `PipelineSegment` | `segment_name` | the `segment_name` property — confirmed correct by §6's own signature query, which already merges/matches on `segment_name` |
| `Person` | `name` | the `name` property (already matches §3 directly) |
| `Incident` | `summary` | the `summary` property — the closest semantic fit; §3 has no `name`-equivalent field for Incident at all, so this is a deliberate pragmatic choice, not a spec-confirmed one like the other three |

## 5. Entity Extraction Pipeline (how nodes/edges get created during ingestion)

1. After chunking (per RAG_SPEC.md §2), run each chunk through a local LLM extraction prompt (use the reasoning sub-agent, `qwen2.5:14b`) with this exact instruction:
```
Extract entities and relationships from the text below. Output ONLY a JSON object with two keys: "entities" (list of {"type": one of ["Equipment","PipelineSegment","Person","Incident"], "name": string, "attributes": object}) and "relationships" (list of {"from": string, "to": string, "type": one of ["REFERENCES","APPLIES_TO","LOCATED_ON","AUTHORED_BY","REPORTS_INCIDENT_AT"]}). Only extract what is explicitly stated in the text. Do not infer relationships that are not directly supported by the text.

TEXT:
{chunk_text}
```
2. Validate extracted `type` values against the fixed lists above — drop anything that doesn't match rather than inventing a new label on the fly
3. Deduplicate entities by normalized name matching (case-insensitive, whitespace-trimmed) before creating new nodes — e.g. "V-204", "v204", "Valve V-204" should resolve to one node; maintain an alias list per entity for this matching, do not silently merge on a fuzzy-match threshold without logging the merge decision to the audit log
4. Create/merge nodes and relationships via Cypher `MERGE` statements (never plain `CREATE`, to avoid duplicate nodes across ingestion runs)

## 6. The Signature Demo Query (implement exactly this, it is the centerpiece graph demo)

**Natural language:** "Show every SOP that references this pipeline segment, and every incident report tied to it."

**Cypher:**
```cypher
MATCH (seg:PipelineSegment {segment_name: $segment_name})
OPTIONAL MATCH (doc:Document)-[:REFERENCES|APPLIES_TO]->(seg)
OPTIONAL MATCH (inc:Incident)-[:REPORTS_INCIDENT_AT]->(seg)
RETURN seg, collect(DISTINCT doc) AS related_documents, collect(DISTINCT inc) AS related_incidents
```

**Demo parameter to use:** `segment_name: "Mangalore-Hassan"` — this is a real named segment of MRPL's actual 363km Petronet MHB pipeline per the MRPL-Grounded Dossier, making the query concrete rather than a toy example with invented data.

**Frontend behavior:** the Graph Explorer (FRONTEND.md §3.6) must visibly highlight the returned subgraph — center the view on `seg`, animate-in the connected `doc` and `inc` nodes, do not just print a text list. The visual "the graph lights up" moment is the actual demo payload, not the underlying Cypher.

## 7. Testing Requirements
- Fixture: a small set of mock SOPs/incident reports mentioning a test pipeline segment and at least 2 equipment tags
- Test asserts: entity extraction correctly identifies the segment and equipment nodes; the signature query returns the expected document/incident set; a document mentioning an entity only in passing (not in an "applicability" section) creates a `REFERENCES` edge, not an `APPLIES_TO` edge — this distinction must be tested explicitly, since collapsing it would misrepresent SOP scope, which matters in a safety context

## 8. Anti-Hallucination Note (graph-specific)
The extraction prompt in §5 explicitly forbids inferring relationships not directly stated in the text. If a document merely mentions a valve tag in passing without an explicit applicability statement, the correct edge is `REFERENCES`, never `APPLIES_TO` — do not let the extraction model or any post-processing step upgrade a passing mention into a scope claim. This distinction is safety-relevant, not pedantic.

# RAG_SPEC.md — Complete Retrieval-Augmented Generation Specification

## 1. Design Principle
Every generated claim in this system must be traceable to a source passage (NFR-4). This document specifies exactly how ingestion, indexing, and retrieval work so that principle is actually enforceable in code, not just aspirational.

## 2. Ingestion Pipeline

**Input types accepted:** PDF (text-native and scanned, per-page — a mixed document with some scanned and some text-native pages is OCR'd only on the pages that actually need it, never the whole document), DOCX, TXT, CSV, XLSX/XLS (each worksheet treated as a numbered "page" for citation purposes), email exports (`.eml`/plain text), scanned TIFF/PNG/JPG (routed through OCR first, per CARD 05 in VIBECODING_SPEC.md), voice notes (`.wav`/`.mp3`/`.m4a`/`.ogg`, routed through local speech-to-text per CARD 12 — **team addition, not PS-traceable, see REQUIREMENTS.md §6**)

**Exact pipeline steps:**
1. **Document type detection** — file extension AND a `python-magic` MIME check, reconciled (don't trust extension alone, but don't trust MIME alone either): MIME overrides a wrong extension, but the extension resolves the specific cases where MIME is provably too generic to trust — OOXML files (.docx/.xlsx) reporting as a bare `application/zip`/`application/octet-stream` on some libmagic builds, and CSV/TXT being byte-identical as `text/plain` (no signature distinguishes them). Both cases are real, observed on this project's own dev machine, not hypothetical.
2. **Text extraction**, per page/sheet (never per whole document — a mixed PDF with some scanned and some text-native pages must only OCR the pages that actually need it):
   - Text-native PDF → `pdfplumber` (preserves layout better than `PyPDF2` for table-heavy refinery documents); any individual page with no extractable text is rendered to an image and routed through CARD 05's OCR pipeline (or its handwritten fallback) for that page only
   - DOCX → `python-docx`'s paragraph/table iteration
   - XLSX → `openpyxl`; XLS (legacy binary) → `xlrd` — each worksheet is one "page" (1-indexed sheet position), so a citation can still say which sheet a fact came from. **Native charts on the sheet are also extracted, exactly, with zero vision model involved** (`backend/ingestion/xlsx_charts.py`): a chart's real values live either in Excel's own cached copy embedded in the chart XML, or (for a chart never opened in real Excel, verified as a real case) are resolved directly from the cell range the chart references — either way this is exact extraction, not description, and is a completely different tool from a chart that only exists as a picture (CARD 13, VIBECODING_SPEC.md — that one genuinely needs a vision model and its output is always labeled an estimate). Requires loading the workbook WITHOUT `read_only=True` — that mode has no chart data at all, verified directly, not assumed.
   - CSV → read as plain text (already delimited, no special parsing needed for chunking)

- CSV → read as plain text (already delimited, no special parsing needed for chunking)
   - Voice notes (.wav/.mp3/.m4a/.ogg) → CARD 12's local speech-to-text, whole recording as one unpaginated "page" — **team addition, not PS-traceable**
3. **Chunking:** recursive character splitter, **chunk size 512 tokens, overlap 64 tokens** (exact values — do not leave these as "reasonable defaults" the agent picks itself; consistency across the corpus matters for retrieval quality comparisons). Use `tiktoken`'s `cl100k_base` encoding to count tokens for the split, even though inference uses local models — it's a good-enough universal tokenizer for chunk-sizing purposes. This is the pipeline's default and the strategy §3's 0.35 confidence threshold is calibrated against.

**Optional alternative — semantic chunking (`backend/ingestion/semantic_chunking.py`):** groups sentences at detected embedding-distance topic-shift boundaries instead of a fixed token count, with the fixed-size splitter above as a safety net for any oversized segment. This is genuinely OPT-IN, not a silent upgrade to the default: switching to it changes the chunk-size distribution the 0.35 threshold assumes, and per this file's own rule, that requires re-tuning and documenting the change here, not swapping it in quietly. Use it deliberately, not by default.
4. **Metadata attached to every chunk (mandatory fields, none optional):**
   ```python
   class ChunkMetadata(BaseModel):
       source_document: str       # original filename
       document_type: str         # sop, inspection_report, correspondence, spec_sheet, etc.
       page_number: int | None    # None only if genuinely unpaginated (e.g. a chat export)
       chunk_index: int           # position within the document
       ingestion_date: str        # ISO 8601
   ```
5. **Embedding:** `BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5` via `sentence-transformers`, batch size 32, normalize embeddings (`normalize_embeddings=True` — required for cosine similarity via FAISS's inner-product index to behave correctly)
6. **Storage:** embeddings → FAISS `IndexFlatIP` (exact index type — flat is fine at hackathon corpus scale, don't over-engineer with IVF/HNSW for a demo-sized corpus); raw chunk text + metadata → a parallel SQLite table keyed by the same chunk ID as the FAISS vector index position

## 3. Retrieval — Hybrid Search (full detail beyond VIBECODING_SPEC CARD 09)

## 3. Retrieval — Hybrid Search (full detail beyond VIBECODING_SPEC CARD 09)

- Dense: FAISS cosine similarity via normalized inner product
- Sparse: BM25Okapi over whitespace-tokenized chunk text
- Fusion: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, k=60, as specified in CARD 09 — this k value is a well-established default from the original RRF paper, not arbitrary, keep it
- **Retrieval confidence threshold:** if the top fused result's normalized score falls below **0.35** (on a 0-1 scale after min-max normalizing the fused scores across the candidate set), the system must return "not found in the provided corpus" rather than passing a weak match to the generation step — this is the literal implementation of the NotebookLM-style refusal behavior from the MRPL Grounded Dossier §2. This threshold is a starting point for tuning during Day 6 testing, not a permanently fixed constant — document any change to it in this file.

## 4. Grounding Enforcement at Generation Time

- The reasoning sub-agent's prompt template must include an explicit instruction block (verbatim, do not paraphrase when implementing):
```
You must only state facts that are directly supported by the SOURCES section below. For every factual claim, include a citation marker [N] referring to the source number. If the sources do not contain enough information to answer, say so explicitly rather than filling the gap from general knowledge.

SOURCES:
{retrieved_chunks_formatted_with_numbers}

REQUEST:
{user_request}
```
- Post-generation validation: parse all `[N]` markers in the output, confirm each `N` corresponds to an actually-retrieved chunk (catches the LLM inventing a citation number that doesn't exist) — if an invalid citation number is found, either strip that claim or flag it for human review before it reaches the approval-note generator; do not silently pass it through

## 5. Contradiction Detection (🟡 tier)
- When two retrieved chunks from different `source_document` values both address the same entity (matched via the graph layer's entity extraction — see GRAPH_SPEC.md) but contain conflicting numeric values or directives, flag both in the UI's citation panel with a visible "⚠ conflicting sources" marker rather than silently picking one

## 6. Version/Revision Awareness (🟡 tier)
- If ingested SOPs carry a revision number/date in their filename or header (extracted via a regex pattern configured per MRPL's actual SOP naming convention — confirm this convention before hardcoding a regex, since PSU documents vary), retrieval should prefer the highest revision number for a given SOP identifier and warn if a lower-revision document is being cited

## 7. Testing Requirements
- A fixture corpus of ≥10 mixed documents (public sample SOPs/reports, per the PS's own dataset note) with 5 known question/expected-answer/expected-source triples
- Test asserts: correct source retrieved in top-3 for all 5; confidence-threshold refusal correctly triggers on an out-of-corpus question (e.g. asking about something not in any ingested document)

# SOURCES_SPEC.md — source tracking, images, and document preview

**Status:** implemented on `aryan/rag-and-graphrag`. This is the contract every
component that touches source documents must follow. Owner: Aryan.

This spec covers four things RAG_SPEC.md §2 does not: where source files live,
how folders are watched, how images inside documents are stored and retrieved,
and how a cited page is shown back to the user.

---

## 1. Core principle: reference, never copy

**The user's files stay where the user put them. We record the path.**

A refinery's document set is gigabytes of PDFs and scans. Copying every ingested
file into a managed store doubles the user's disk for no benefit — the bytes are
already on the machine. Everything downstream (previews, "open the source",
extracting a figure) reads the original file in place, on demand.

The one exception is **images extracted from inside documents** (§3): those are
stored, because they do not exist as files anywhere and cannot be re-derived
without re-parsing the document every time one is displayed.

### Consequences the whole team must handle

Referencing files we do not own means they can move, change, or vanish. That is
**normal operation, not an error** — a user moves a folder, a share unmounts,
someone edits an SOP after it was indexed. `DocumentRegistry.resolve()` therefore
returns a **status**, never an exception:

| status | meaning | what the UI must say |
|---|---|---|
| `available` | present, unchanged since indexing | nothing special |
| `modified` | present, bytes differ from what was indexed | "this file changed since it was indexed; quoted text may no longer match" |
| `missing` | recorded path holds no file | "moved or deleted after indexing — re-add it to restore previews" |
| `unknown` | never registered | treat as not ingested |

Never silently show nothing. A wrong-but-confident citation is the failure mode
this whole design exists to prevent.

---

## 2. Watched sources — `backend/ingestion/source_watcher.py`

A user adds a **path**, not a file: `Downloads`, a project folder, a mounted
share. Anything ingestible appearing under it becomes searchable without being
added again.

---

## 2. Watched sources — `backend/ingestion/source_watcher.py`

A user adds a **path**, not a file: `Downloads`, a project folder, a mounted
share. Anything ingestible appearing under it becomes searchable without being
added again.

### Scanning, not filesystem events

Deliberate. OS watch APIs (`inotify`, `ReadDirectoryChangesW`) are
platform-specific, silently lossy on network shares, and miss everything that
happened while the app was closed — which for a desktop workbench is most of the
time. Scanning is predictable, testable, identical on every platform, and cannot
miss an overnight change. A watch API may later feed the same queue as an
optimisation, never as a replacement.

### What a scan classifies

| kind | test | action |
|---|---|---|
| new | path not in registry | ingest |
| modified | size **or** mtime differs | **re-ingest** — old chunks describe text that is gone |
| unchanged | size and mtime match | skip, cheaply |

**Scans use size + mtime only — never a hash.** On a Downloads folder with
thousands of files almost everything is unchanged, and hashing every file to
learn that is a scan nobody will leave enabled. Hashing happens once, at
registration. A file touched but not edited costs one wasted re-ingest; that is
the accepted trade.

### Exclusions (`SUPPORTED_SUFFIXES`, `EXCLUDE_PATTERNS`)

Only formats RAG_SPEC §2 can actually read are offered. Also always excluded:
Office lock files (`~$*`), partial downloads (`*.crdownload`, `*.part`), OS
metadata (`Thumbs.db`, `.DS_Store`), and anything under a dot-directory.
**Ingesting a half-written download produces garbage chunks that then have to be
hunted down**, which is worse than ingesting it late.

---

## 3. Priority: newest modification time first

**One ordering key delivers the entire policy.**

A file that just arrived has the newest mtime, so it sorts ahead of everything —
new work preempts the backlog automatically. The backlog then drains
most-recent-first, which is also correct: last quarter's report is likelier to be
asked about than one from four years ago.

There is deliberately **no separate "new vs backlog" bookkeeping**, because a

### Queue — `backend/ingestion/ingestion_queue.py`

Durable, because a Downloads folder can present thousands of files each costing
seconds to minutes (OCR, transcription, figure description). Must survive the app
closing mid-run.

States: `pending → in_progress → done | failed`.

- **Failures are state, not exceptions.** One corrupt PDF must not stall the queue
  behind it, must not retry forever, and must not vanish silently. Retried
  `MAX_ATTEMPTS` (3) times, then parked as `failed` with its error, where a UI can
  show it and `requeue_failed()` can retry after the user fixes the cause.
- **Re-scanning must not reset attempt counts**, or a broken file retries forever.
- **Storage is append-only JSON-Lines with `fsync`**, compacted atomically. Same
  reasoning as `extract_corpus.py`: a rewritten file loses everything if the
  process dies mid-write; one line per state change costs at most that line.

---

## 4. Images inside documents

### 4.1 Every image gets BOTH kinds of understanding

For each image found in any document, the pipeline records:

1. **OCR text** — what is *written in* it (CARD 05). For a P&ID this is
   `V-204, E-201B, K-201` — exactly the tokens an engineer types into search.
2. **Vision description** — what it *depicts* (CARD 13). "Hydrocracker reactor
   loop with recycle gas compressor."

**Both, always — never one chosen by guessing the image type.** They answer
different questions and neither subsumes the other: a description paraphrases
away the tags OCR captures, and OCR can never produce the description. Guessing
drops whichever the guess got wrong.

### 4.2 Both go into the chunk text

### 4.2 Both go into the chunk text

`render_image_block()` produces the text that stands in for the image inside the
chunk, so the image is reachable by ordinary retrieval:

```
[Image 1 on page 3 — ref image:a1b2c3d4e5f6]
Text visible in the image: V-204 E-201B K-201 Reactor Stripper
Description of the image (vision-model estimate, not a measurement): A piping and
instrumentation diagram of the hydrocracker reactor loop...
```

**The estimate caveat is inline in the indexed text, not only in metadata.** If a
consumer renders chunk text and drops metadata — a prompt, a log line, a paste
into a report — the caveat must travel with the words or it is lost exactly where
it matters most. See §4.5.

### 4.3 Storage is content-addressed — `backend/ingestion/image_store.py`

Keyed by SHA-256 of the pixels. **This is load-bearing, not tidiness.** Real
corpora repeat images constantly — letterheads, standard safety diagrams, the
same equipment photo in six reports. Content-addressing means:

- each distinct image is described **once** (a vision call is tens of seconds);
- "the same image" is a fact about the bytes, not a guess from filename;
- one image with N **occurrences** (document, page, bbox), not N copies.

Metadata is a **sidecar JSON per image**, not one shared index: ingestion is
incremental and interruptible, and a shared index needs read-modify-write and
locking to be crash-safe. A file per image is atomic per image.

### 4.4 Chunks carry image ids

`ChunkMetadata.image_ids` lists every image on the page the chunk came from.
**Every chunk from a page inherits that page's images** — a chunk is a slice of
text, but the image belongs to the page, and attaching it only to whichever slice
contains the description block makes it unreachable from the others.

### 4.5 Retrieving the right image — `backend/retrieval/image_retrieval.py`

### 4.5 Retrieving the right image — `backend/retrieval/image_retrieval.py`

A page holds several images, so a chunk references several. **Returning all of
them is not an answer.** `select_images_for_request()` embeds the user's request
and each image's combined understanding (source name + description + OCR) and
ranks them, so:

- "show me the hydrocracker schematic" → the P&ID, via its description
- "the diagram with V-204 on it" → the P&ID, via its OCR text
- "the downtime chart" → the bar chart

**Returns empty rather than a weak best guess** below `MIN_IMAGE_MATCH_SIMILARITY`.
Always returning the top match means a question that referenced no image still
produces one, which reads as a claim that the picture is relevant. Putting the
wrong diagram in front of an engineer is worse than attaching none.

### 4.6 Hard constraint #3 applies to every chart reading

`description_is_estimate` is `True` on every record and must survive to the point
of display. **This is measured, not theoretical:** on generated charts carrying
*no printed numbers at all*, the vision model emitted specific figures and
described them as values "printed as text on the chart" — 10 invented values
across 2 of 6 charts (`backend/evaluation/CHART_STRESS_REPORT.md`). A UI that
renders one of those like a measurement defeats the constraint.

## 5. Document preview — `backend/retrieval/document_preview.py`

An answer citing "SOP-114, page 7" is a claim the user cannot check without going
to find it. In a 500-page document that friction is why people stop trusting
retrieval. **Show the page, with the passage highlighted.**

An answer citing "SOP-114, page 7" is a claim the user cannot check without going
to find it. In a 500-page document that friction is why people stop trusting
retrieval. **Show the page, with the passage highlighted.**

- `preview_for_chunk(chunk, registry)` → rendered PNG of that page + highlight
  rectangles **in image pixel space**.
- **Only one page is ever rendered.** Rendering is the expensive step; a preview
  needs the page asked about, not the document. One page at 150 DPI is a few
  hundred KB and tens of milliseconds.
- Coordinates are converted from PDF points to pixels **here**, because the
  conversion depends on the DPI this module chose, and a consumer that has to
  know that will eventually get it wrong.

### Highlights are searched for, never stored

Storing character offsets at ingestion would be faster, but they go stale the
moment the document is edited and would then highlight the wrong region **with
total confidence** — worse than no highlight. Searching the live page either
matches what is there now, or honestly finds nothing.

Anchoring tries phrases from several positions in the chunk (start, third,
middle), because a chunk usually spans a page boundary at one end, so any single
anchor position fails often.

### Unpaginated sources return `None`

DOCX, TXT, email and audio have no page. Rendering "page 1" of a flow document
would show something the text may not be on. `page_number is None` is a real
property of the format, not missing data — never fabricate one.

| module | responsibility |
|---|---|
| `ingestion/document_registry.py` | where each source file lives; identity and change status |
| `ingestion/source_watcher.py` | watched folders; classify new/modified/unchanged |

## 7. Invariants — do not break these without updating this file

1. **Never copy a user's source document.** Record the path.
2. **Never fabricate a page number** for an unpaginated format.
3. **Never present a vision description as a measurement.** The estimate flag
   travels to the point of display, including inside indexed chunk text.
4. **Never return a best-guess image** below the similarity floor. Return none.
5. **Never hash every file on a routine scan.** Size + mtime; hash at registration.
6. **Never reset a queue item's attempt count on re-scan.**
7. **Failed ingestions stay visible.** Silent failure means "why is this document
   not searchable?" has no answer.
